title: 10 Truths 25+ Years of Entrepreneurship Taught Me (the Hard Way)
author: Summer Mulder
summary: Mulder frames this list against her own recent shift from running one company, which she describes as her identity until it was not, to helping lead growth across nine home service businesses under a holding company. The ten lessons that follow are operational rather than motivational. Several concern focus and measurement: stuck teams are usually solving the wrong problem because the scoreboard is wrong, a calendar reveals what a leader actually values, and distraction is the most expensive line item in a business. Others concern exposure, notably her claim that installing a scorecard, an accountability cadence and a clear goal immediately reveals who steps up, who checks out and who has been good at looking busy. She warns that growth amplifies dysfunction rather than solving it, so unclear teams and reactive communication get ten times worse at ten times the revenue. On cash she is blunt, separating revenue on paper from profit that keeps the lights on from cash in the bank that lets you sleep. Her view of good operating is deliberately unexciting, consisting of weekly scorecard reviews, quarterly priorities and unchanging meeting cadences. The final note is that most plans were fine and simply were not stuck with long enough.
points: The scoreboard claim reframes team performance problems as measurement problems, since teams tracking metrics that do not matter will keep avoiding the real constraint.

Mulder's test for leadership quality is whether an operator asks better questions rather than gives faster answers, with three specific prompts about what is really going on and what the actual constraint is.
Her warning that growth amplifies dysfunction rather than resolving it argues for cleaning up communication and systems at $1M rather than waiting for $10M.
The three-way distinction between revenue, profit and cash in the bank is the sharpest financial line in the list, with cash cast as what actually lets an owner sleep.
She characterises real success as boring, consisting of unchanging meeting cadences and repeating the same things better, which is an argument against novelty-seeking driven by ego.
quotes: I’ve walked into “stuck” teams only to realize they were tracking metrics that didn’t matter and avoiding the one constraint that actually needed fixing. The right scoreboard reveals the real constraint.
I watched one CEO sit in meetings for 6 hours straight. Only 15 minutes of that entire day moved the needle.
Put in a scorecard, an accountability cadence, and a clear goal and suddenly you see who steps up, who checks out, and who’s just been good at looking busy.
Focus isn’t sexy. It’s saying no to the next cool thing again and again until what’s working becomes world-class.
If the team is unclear, the systems are messy, and the communication is reactive at $1M… expect it to be 10x worse at $10M. Clean it up early.
Most businesses aren’t broken. The plan was fine. They just didn’t stick with it long enough to see the payoff.
Leading multiple companies at once has taught me that simplicity is a superpower.
